content: Nyctophobia, derived from the Greek words nyx (meaning night) and phobia (meaning fear), is a pathological fear of darkness. It is also referred to as scotophobia (from the Greek skotos, meaning darkness), lygophobia (from lyge, meaning twilight), or noctiphobia. Individuals suffering from nyctophobia experience an abnormal and persistent fear of the dark, often accompanied by significant anxiety. This fear persists even when the individual is fully aware, on a rational level, that darkness does not inherently pose a significant threat. Treatment options for nyctophobia are similar to those used for other specific phobias and may include therapeutic interventions such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure therapy, or, in some cases, pharmacological treatments to manage anxiety symptoms. Nyctophobia is most commonly observed in children, although it can also affect adults. It is worth noting that this condition plays a central role in the plot of Isaac Asimov's short story Nightfall, where the fear of darkness is explored in a fictional context.
